title: If you only have a single class A, how can you prove it follows OOP principles (encapsulation, abstraction, polymorphism via overloading, inheritance via Object)?
shortTitle: How can a single class prove it follows OOP principles?
keyPoints: Encapsulation: private fields with validated public methods prove data protection in a single class
Abstraction: public methods hide private helper methods, exposing what but not how
Polymorphism (compile-time): method overloading within the same class gives multiple forms of the same method name
Polymorphism (runtime): overriding toString(), equals(), hashCode() from Object proves dynamic dispatch
Inheritance: every Java class implicitly extends java.lang.Object, inheriting 11 methods
All four pillars are structural properties of every Java class, not patterns you apply externally

s1_definition.oneliner: A single class proves all four pillars: private fields (encapsulation), public-hides-private methods (abstraction), overloaded methods (compile-time polymorphism), and implicit extends Object with overridden toString/equals (runtime polymorphism via inheritance).
s1_definition.profdef:
Even a single class with no explicit `extends`, no interfaces, and no sibling classes demonstrates all four OOP pillars.

- **Encapsulation** is proven by `private` fields and `public` methods that validate access. There is no `setBalance()`: the balance changes only through `deposit()` and `withdraw()`.
- **Abstraction** is proven by `public` methods (WHAT) that hide `private` helper methods (HOW). The caller sees `deposit(amount)` but not the five internal steps.
- **Compile-time polymorphism** is proven by method overloading: `deposit(BigDecimal)`, `deposit(BigDecimal, String)`, and `deposit(BigDecimal, String, String)` share the same name but different parameter lists.
- **Runtime polymorphism and inheritance** are proven because every class implicitly extends `java.lang.Object`. Overriding `toString()`, `equals()`, and `hashCode()` means the JVM dispatches to the child's version at runtime through an `Object` reference.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has only one type of account: just BankAccount. No SavingsAccount, no CurrentAccount. Can this single class still be object-oriented? Yes. Encapsulation: balance is private, only deposit and withdraw can change it. Abstraction: deposit(amount) hides the five internal steps (validate, update, log, notify, audit). Polymorphism: deposit(1000) and deposit(1000, "Salary credit") are the same name with different parameters. Inheritance: BankAccount implicitly extends Object, and you override toString() to print "SAV2001: Rs.125000" instead of "BankAccount@1a2b3c".

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BankAccount (single class)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ENCAPSULATION                               │
  │  private String accountId                    │
  │  private BigDecimal balance                  │
  │  No setBalance()                             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ABSTRACTION                                 │
  │  public deposit(amount) ← caller sees this   │
  │    private validatePositive()                 │
  │    private updateBalance()   ← hidden         │
  │    private logTransaction()                   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  COMPILE-TIME POLYMORPHISM                   │
  │  deposit(BigDecimal)                         │
  │  deposit(BigDecimal, String)                 │
  │  deposit(BigDecimal, String, String)         │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  INHERITANCE + RUNTIME POLYMORPHISM          │
  │  extends Object (implicit)                   │
  │  @Override toString()                        │
  │  @Override equals(Object)                    │
  │  @Override hashCode()                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Even a single class with no explicit extends or implements demonstrates all four OOP pillars. Encapsulation: private fields like balance can only be changed through public methods like deposit() and withdraw() that validate every modification. There is no setBalance() method. Abstraction: the public deposit() method hides three private steps (validatePositive, updateBalance, logTransaction). The caller knows what happens (deposit money) but not how it happens internally. Polymorphism has two forms in a single class: compile-time via method overloading (three deposit methods with different parameters, the compiler chooses the correct one based on arguments) and runtime via Object inheritance (overriding toString, equals, and hashCode, where the JVM dispatches to the BankAccount version at runtime when called through an Object reference).

In Rajesh's BankAccount class at National Bank of India, deposit(5000), deposit(5000, "Salary"), and deposit(5000, "Salary", "NEFT-REF") are three overloaded methods: compile-time polymorphism. account.toString() returns "SAV2001: Rs.125000" instead of Object's default "BankAccount@1a2b3c": this is runtime polymorphism because the JVM dispatches to the overridden method based on the actual object type. HashSet correctly deduplicates accounts by accountId because equals() and hashCode() are overridden from Object: proving both inheritance and polymorphism.

Remember one sentence: OOP is not something you add to a class; it is a fundamental property of every Java class through private fields, public methods, overloaded signatures, and implicit inheritance from Object.
